model.comments: High effort Claude Fable 5.1. Thinking is always on for Fable; depth is controlled by Anthropic's output_config.effort, which OpenRouter sets from reasoning.effort (its verbosity field maps to the same native field, so this equals the older opus-4.x verbosity convention).

prompt: # Role - You are an AI competing in a gaming arena. # Objective - Write a complete Python file that provides the next move for a game of Go on a 19x19 board. - You must define a smart policy that is able to beat other policies in the arena. - You will be disqualified if you do not return a legal move string. Therefore, you must always return a legal move string. # Required API The provided python file must implement the following API: ```python def policy(me: list[tuple[int, int]], opponent: list[tuple[int, int]]) -> tuple[int, int]: ... ``` # State Representation - You are always the player to move. - `me` is a list of (row, col) tuples containing your stones. - `opponent` is a list of (row, col) tuples containing the opponent's stones. - Rows are indexed from 1 (top) to 19 (bottom). - Columns are indexed from 1 (left) to 19 (right). # Action / Return Format - Return exactly ONE move as a tuple `(row, col)`. - Use `(0, 0)` to pass. # Constraints - You may use any standard Python imports, including numpy. - Your code is allowed 1 second of execution time on a modern 3GHz CPU. # Output Format Requirements - Output your strategy before providing the Python source code for your policy. - Output the Python source code for your policy surrounded by `...` tags. # Example Output The strategy for this policy is... ...
reasoning:
Since the board state has no move history, I can't detect ko directly, so I'm considering a heuristic instead: avoiding moves that capture exactly one stone when the capturing stone itself ends up with only one liberty, since that shape often indicates a ko fight.

Passing is always a safe legal fallback, but too many passes will hurt performance, so I'm leaning toward simply excluding these ko-shaped recaptures rather than eliminating everything else. I'll build the move selection around a heuristic evaluating captures and group safety at one ply deep.

Given the one-second time budget and 361 candidate points, I need efficient flood-fill-based group detection to keep evaluation fast in pure Python—computing legality by checking empty neighbors, capture potential, and connection to friendly groups with multiple liberties, then simulating each candidate move to check resulting liberties and captures.

For scoring, I'm weighing capture count heavily, penalizing self-atari unless it captures, rewarding moves that rescue groups in atari or put opponent groups in atari (especially when the opponent's escape would leave them with few liberties), and factoring in overall liberty reduction plus an influence-based territory estimate using distance-decay kernels around stones to approximate how the board's currently divided.

I also want opening heuristics -- avoiding the first line, favoring third/fourth line and corner play, penalizing self-atari eye-filling moves where all neighbors are already mine, and passing only once no move yields a positive score.

Since scoring rules affect whether filling own territory costs points, I'll be conservative and only heavily penalize moves that fill fully-surrounded own points, treating dame filling as harmless. I also want a shallow ladder reader that simulates opponent extensions to check whether a chased group ends up captured within a limited depth, and logic for defending my own groups in atari by evaluating extension safety.

For performance, I'm avoiding a full board flood fill per candidate move by tracking liberties incrementally—merging adjacent friendly groups' liberty sets and adjusting for captures only when they actually occur, since that's rare enough to recompute fully.

I realize I can avoid copying the board entirely by tracking group ids and liberty sets, updating merged liberties incrementally for candidate moves and captures, saving explicit ladder simulation for only the tricky cases. For influence estimation, I'll use numpy with a distance-weighted kernel centered on each stone, summing contributions to approximate territory at empty points.

For move gains, I'm computing capture and self-atari penalties: captures score highly (roughly 8 per stone plus bonus), self-atari without a capture is almost always disallowed, and I need to special-case single-stone captures that create ko-like shapes to avoid illegal moves. I'm also assigning moderate penalties for moves that leave only two liberties, scaled by group size.

Beyond that, I'm building a rescue bonus: if a friendly group in atari gains two or more liberties after the move (including captures), it earns a bonus proportional to its size, since saving valuable stones is worth roughly the same as capturing them. I'm also planning to evaluate ataris placed on opponent groups by checking whether their single remaining liberty lets them escape via extension, which requires a quick simulation of their response.

For opponent groups, I want tiered bonuses based on escape difficulty — heavy bonus if they truly can't escape, moderate if a ladder situation arises, small if they can just run. Then reducing libs from 3 to 2 gets a small bonus, growing a friendly group's liberties from 2 to 4+ gets a bonus, connecting two groups is worth a flat bonus, and filling my own eye is heavily penalized. I'm also setting edge/second-line penalties that matter more in the opening, and starting to think about preferred opening points on the 3-4 line when few stones are on the board.

I'm adding an explicit corner bonus for empty corner points beyond what the influence kernel captures, plus a smaller bonus for empty third/fourth line points on the sides, with a tiny random tie-breaker. For passing, I'm setting a threshold so that if the best scoring move is below it, I pass — filling dame is neutral under area scoring, and playing inside my own territory with no adjacent opponent stones yields zero gain, which naturally leads to passing there while still responding if the opponent invades.

I also want to guard against reducing large groups adjacent to opponents down to two liberties carelessly, and handle ko/snapback nuances: capturing multiple stones while leaving my own stone at one liberty is fine since I still net a gain, though I'll penalize it slightly since it invites recapture. Finally, I'm sketching a ladder-reading helper that checks whether a group in atari can escape by counting resulting liberties after the escape move — three or more liberties means it likely escapes, zero means it can't (unless it's a capturing move).

For the case of two resulting liberties, I need to try chasing at each liberty, making sure my chasing stone isn't self-atari, and recurse with a depth limit; I also need to check if the group can escape by capturing one of my own low-liberty groups instead. For implementation, I'm representing the board as a flat array of intersections with precomputed neighbor lists, along with flood-fill and play functions that handle captures, and I'm capping the ladder search with depth and node limits to keep it efficient given how many atari candidates could trigger a search.

I'm adding a time-based deadline check so expensive ladder reads get skipped if I'm running low on budget. For defending my own atari'd groups, I need a similar recursive escape-checker that considers extending toward a liberty or capturing an adjacent attacker group that's itself in atari, treating anything past the depth limit as an assumed escape to stay conservative.

For the attacker side, I'm mirroring this with a capture-checker that tries each liberty, skips moves that would self-atari, and recurses if the defender's group drops back to one liberty. I still need to weight captured stones and territory shifts numerically, roughly valuing each stone highly and giving smaller credit to territory flips, to score how costly a failed ladder escape actually is.

Now I'm thinking about opening-move heuristics: giving bonus points to empty corner star-points like 3-3, 3-4, 4-4, and applying line-based adjustments (small bonuses for third and fourth lines, penalties for first and second lines) while stone count stays low. I'm also sketching an influence kernel that weights points by Manhattan distance from a stone, giving higher weight near the stone and tapering off further away.

I should add a penalty for playing inside strongly opponent-influenced regions unless it's tactically justified, and similarly penalize playing deep in my own territory except for tactical reasons. I also want to boost moves that give breathing room to weak groups with only two liberties, plus reward saving groups in atari or capturing, and I should avoid recommending moves that fill in my own eye shapes.

For pass logic, I'm thinking to pass when the best available score dips below roughly 0.5, but I need to be careful since line-1 endgame moves can matter late in the game even if they look weak — so I want to scale down the line-based penalty as the game progresses, tapering it based on how many stones are on the board.

I still need to guard against moves that walk into a ladder — for candidates with only two liberties, I'll run a quick ladder check to see if the resulting group gets captured, but only for the top handful of candidates to keep things fast. I'll also handle capture-heavy moves properly: if playing a stone would remove an opponent group's last liberty, I should simulate the actual capture and reflood liberties afterward rather than just approximating with a set union, since that's the only case where a plain merge undercounts.

Now I'm starting to write the implementation.

Writing board and move logic...

Still writing ladder logic...

I'm double-checking edge cases: whether captures during defender's escape attempt actually free up liberties, and whether the attacker's play could accidentally capture other groups rather than the target. These seem handled correctly since captures always add liberties.

For the main policy function, I'm building the board representation from stone lists, computing groups, then figuring out territorial influence using a convolution-style approach — padding the board and summing weighted shifts across a Manhattan-distance kernel to avoid needing scipy, so I can quickly evaluate how each candidate move shifts the influence map.

I decide to vectorize by stacking 361 kernel slices (one per board point) so I can compute the influence gain for every candidate move in one batch operation, using thresholds to classify points as owned, contested, or opponent territory, then converting that into penalty/bonus scores that get combined with tactical bonuses like captures and ataris in the final move-scoring loop.

Now I'm working through the per-point move evaluation: for each empty point I gather friendly and enemy neighboring groups, check for captures (opponent groups reduced to one liberty), simulate the placement to count resulting liberties and stone count, handle ko and suicide exclusions, then build a score combining territory gain, capture bonuses, and heavy self-atari penalties — though I still need to work out the right penalty for a lone stone self-atari that otherwise sits in a valuable spot.

I'm continuing to flesh out the scoring heuristic: penalizing low-liberty results (with reduced penalty if it comes with a capture, since snapback risk still applies), rewarding rescuing my own groups that are in atari or near-atari when the new move gives enough liberties, and rewarding placing atari on enemy two-liberty groups — but only after verifying with a reader/escape-check that the opponent can't simply capture back or ladder free.

Beyond captures, I'm adding connection bonuses for linking two of my groups, an eye-filling penalty to discourage destroying my own eyes, and edge/line-based adjustments so first- and second-line moves are penalized while third/fourth-line points get a small bonus. Early in the game I also want a bonus for playing near open corners and star points to encourage standard opening shape, plus deeper territorial scoring adjustments from the influence map.

For move selection, after scoring I take the top candidates and specifically verify that any group left with only two liberties can't be immediately captured by a ladder-style attack, penalizing heavily if so. I also need to decide the passing threshold carefully—since penalties like the line-1 penalty can make otherwise decent endgame moves look negative, so I'm tuning those penalty magnitudes down to avoid passing prematurely when good territory-gaining moves still exist.

I want to add defensive checks for my own weak groups with two liberties, running a limited ladder-capture check (capped at 600 nodes to respect time budget) and marking endangered groups so that saving moves get properly rewarded. Similarly, I should flag opponent groups with two liberties that are ladder-capturable so atari moves against them get bonus scoring, though I need to keep this bounded given time constraints.

To keep things fast, I'm capping ladder read node limits to around 400 and enforcing a global deadline check before running any read, skipping ladder analysis entirely once the deadline passes. I also want a final safety check that simulates the chosen move to confirm it's legal and has liberties, falls back to the next candidate if not, and handles the ko rule and empty-candidate edge cases with a reasonable default move.

For eye-filling avoidance, I'm relying on the deep-territory penalty to discourage filling points deep inside owned territory unless tactical captures justify it, and using a ladder-based penalty to offset the bonus for extending groups that are still doomed to be captured. I'm also making sure atari-response bonuses for opponent groups require at least two liberties to avoid triggering self-atari.

Writing influence-based territory scoring...

The threshold for counting a point as "owned" or "opponent" territory is set at 1.5, with distance-1 weights possibly bumped up to make adjacent moves feel more impactful — this influence gain metric should end up favoring moves along the boundary between contested territories where flipping control is still possible.

I want to add a corner bonus: checking if the 7x7 corner region is still empty early in the game and rewarding moves there, plus a smaller bonus for side/third-line points once the corners fill up, though the influence calculation might already capture some of this naturally. I'm also thinking through how the flood-fill logic for territory should work once approach moves start contesting the corners.

Now I'm setting up the core board representation and policy function, initializing the board array from the move lists and mapping opponent stones onto it.

I'm computing an influence map using a convolution kernel over the stone positions, then measuring how many points would newly fall under each player's territory for each candidate move.

Now I'm identifying own groups with only two liberties as endangered, so I can check whether an opponent's capture-reading confirms the threat before deadline expires.

I'm working out how to compute each move's board line (distance from edge) for scoring purposes, then adding a safety check: penalize moves that reduce a friendly group's liberties down to two or fewer through connection or extension.

Now I'm scaling that penalty by group size for two-liberty groups so bigger endangered groups get a stronger penalty, while still letting the atari-saving bonus dominate when it matters. I'm also making sure the ko-shape skip logic applies during verification, not just candidate generation, and confirming the performance is fine since I'm only checking a few hundred candidates with set unions.

Writing the flood-fill helper...

I'm also double-checking a subtlety in the attacker capture logic — captured defender stones can't belong to the two-liberty defender group itself since that would require it to already have fewer liberties, and any removed stones adjacent to it would just be counted as part of the same group. In `defender_escapes`, playing on a liberty correctly recomputes the liberty count after any captures that result from that move.

For the top-K refinement step, I'm building the board after the candidate move lazily, then checking if the attacker can still capture even after the defender's escape attempt, penalizing the score heavily if so and re-sorting the candidates. Then for deciding whether to pass, I'm using a simple threshold: if the best remaining score is too low, just pass rather than force a bad play.

But I realize there's a subtlety with scoring rules that assume all stones are alive (area scoring without dead stone removal) -- in that case, leaving an opponent's dead group sitting inside my territory is actually costly, since those stones still count as territory-neutral or even opponent points unless physically captured. This means the influence map needs to treat an enemy stone embedded in my area as strongly negative, spreading that negativity to neighboring points so they're seen as contested rather than safely mine.

I should also add a general bonus for reducing liberties of any adjacent opponent group, scaling with group size, and give a strong bonus when an opponent group is in atari with no escape.

Under Tromp-Taylor scoring, empty points touching both colors count as neutral, so surrounding dead stones still matters. I'll set a pass threshold where the best move scoring below 0.1 triggers a pass, and I'm weighing how the deep-territory penalty interacts with tactical responses to a 4-liberty opponent stone placed inside my territory.

I feel comfortable with the reasoning now — time to write the code.
